name: Iwan David Herstatt

summary.text: Iwan David Herstatt was the co-owner and namesake of Bankhaus I.D. Herstatt KGaA of Cologne. On the afternoon of 26 June 1974 the German authorities ordered the bank into liquidation after large foreign-exchange losses. Because the bank was closed after the German banking day but while the New York business day was still open, counterparties that had already paid Deutsche marks in Frankfurt did not receive the dollars owed to them; this settlement exposure became known as 'Herstatt risk'. Herstatt himself was later prosecuted in Cologne and, according to a German trade-union foundation magazine, received a two-year suspended sentence.

sources.title: Uncovering FX settlement risk: new measures from the 2025 BIS Triennial Survey

facts.claim: On the afternoon of 26 June 1974 the German authorities ordered Bankhaus Herstatt into liquidation; the bank was closed at 3.30 pm Frankfurt time, after which its New York correspondent bank suspended all outgoing US dollar payments from Herstatt's account.
facts.quote: On the afternoon of 26 June 1974, the German authorities ordered Bankhaus Herstatt into liquidation. The bank was closed at 3.30 pm Frankfurt time, after which its New York correspondent bank suspended all outgoing US dollar payments from Herstatt's account.

sources.title: Uncovering FX settlement risk: new measures from the 2025 BIS Triennial Survey

facts.claim: Herstatt's counterparties were left exposed for the full value of the Deutsche marks they had already paid in Frankfurt earlier that day to settle dollar-mark foreign exchange trades; the Basel Committee describes the result as a total loss of principal for those counterparties, a form of risk that became known as 'Herstatt risk'.
facts.quote: this form of credit risk, known as delivery risk (but naturally enough quickly enshrined as "Herstatt risk") resulted in a total loss of principal for Herstatt's counterparties.

sources.title: Uncovering FX settlement risk: new measures from the 2025 BIS Triennial Survey

facts.claim: The Bank of England's archive study of the failure notes that the German supervisor acted after the close of banking business in Germany but, because of the time difference, still during the business day in the United States, and that banks in other countries then delayed settling payments to each other.
facts.quote: the Supervisor's action occurred after close of banking business in Germany, but (because of the time difference) still during the business day in the US.

sources.publisher: Bank Underground (Bank of England staff blog)
sources.title: BoE archives reveal little known lesson from the 1974 failure of Herstatt Bank

facts.claim: The European Central Bank's account of the episode states that a counterparty had already received, via the German payment system, the marks it had bought, while Herstatt had not yet delivered the dollars it had sold because of the time-zone difference.
facts.quote: by this time, it had already received – via the German payment system – the marks it had bought two days earlier. However, because of the time zone difference, Bankhaus Herstatt had not yet delivered the dollars it had sold.

facts.claim: According to the Hans-Böckler-Stiftung's magazine, Iwan D. Herstatt was sentenced to two years' probation (a suspended sentence), while chief currency trader Dany Dattel was regarded as the principal offender but was declared unfit to stand trial and never received a verdict.
facts.quote: Iwan D. Herstatt is sentenced to two years' probation. Dany Dattel is considered the principal offender, but he is declared unfit to stand trial.

facts.claim: The same magazine reports that Hans Gerling, chairman of the bank's supervisory board and its main shareholder, was not among the defendants, and that prosecutors considered his approval of the currency speculation not criminally relevant.
facts.quote: The chairman of the supervisory board and main shareholder of the Herstatt Bank, insurance executive Hans Gerling, was missing from the list of defendants.

facts.claim: The BIS notes that the Herstatt failure led to work on payment-versus-payment settlement for foreign exchange, now provided through CLS Bank, and that more than fifty years later FX settlement risk remains a live concern.
facts.quote: more than 50 years have passed since the failure of Bankhaus Herstatt, yet more remains to be done

sources.title: Uncovering FX settlement risk: new measures from the 2025 BIS Triennial Survey

connections.claim: Hans Gerling, an insurance executive, was the main shareholder of Bankhaus Herstatt and chairman of its supervisory board; he was not charged in the Cologne prosecution.
connections.quote: The chairman of the supervisory board and main shareholder of the Herstatt Bank, insurance executive Hans Gerling, was missing from the list of defendants.

connections.claim: Dany Dattel was the bank's chief currency trader; he was regarded as the principal offender in the foreign-exchange losses but was declared unfit to stand trial.
connections.quote: Dany Dattel is considered the principal offender, but he is declared unfit to stand trial.

openQuestions: The sentence against Iwan David Herstatt: the Böckler magazine gives two years' probation without a court or date; one popular source says a 1976 fine of DM 60,000 plus a suspended sentence; an AI-generated encyclopedia says the Cologne Regional Court imposed four and a half years in 1984, reduced to two years' probation on appeal. The owner should check a German court record or a Spiegel/Zeit archive before publishing a date.
The site's loss figure of DM 470-500 million appears only in a popular history site in the results returned; no central-bank source returned gave a loss figure.
The site's claims that counterparties lost an estimated $620 million and that around 38,000 depositors had funds frozen were not found in the sources returned.

The site's claim that US banks held back CHIPS payments: the ECB box states the CHIPS system had to close for a day, and the BIS describes payment gridlock, but the exact CHIPS mechanics should be read in the ECB and New York Fed documents (a 1996 New York Fed speech on FX settlement risk was returned but not read in detail).
